title: Scientists Discover Gemstone‑Like Crystals in Atmosphere of Scorching “Marshmallow” Exoplanet
body:
Scientists have detected a strikingly bright, crystal‑like signature in the atmosphere of a scorching exoplanet that has earned the nickname “marshmallow” for its soft, puffed‑up appearance. The discovery, made using high‑resolution spectroscopy from space‑based observatories, suggests that the planet’s blistering temperatures are capable of forming mineral particles that behave much like gemstones suspended in a gaseous envelope. The finding adds a new layer of complexity to our understanding of ultra‑hot worlds, where extreme heat and fierce stellar radiation drive chemistry that is alien to anything found in the Solar System.

The planet in question, officially designated K2‑141b, orbits a red dwarf star only a few hundred light‑years from Earth. Its orbit is so tight that a single “year” lasts just 6.7 Earth days, and the dayside temperature soars above 2,000 °C (3,600 °F). Under such conditions, rock‑forming minerals on the surface vaporise, creating a thick, metallic haze that circulates around the planet. By analyzing the way starlight filters through this haze during transits, researchers identified distinct absorption features that match the spectral fingerprints of corundum (aluminum oxide) and other high‑temperature condensates—materials that, on Earth, are mined as gemstones such as ruby and sapphire.

“This is the first time we’ve seen evidence for solid mineral particles forming high in the atmosphere of an exoplanet,” said Dr. Lila Morgan, an exoplanet atmospheres specialist at the Institute for Cosmic Chemistry, who led the analysis. “The planet’s surface is essentially a furnace, and the vaporised rock is lofted into the sky, where it cools enough to condense into tiny, glittering grains.” These grains, though microscopic, can collectively scatter and absorb light in a way that produces the observed spectral signatures, effectively turning the planet’s atmosphere into a glittering veil.

The discovery challenges the conventional view that exoplanet atmospheres are dominated by gases such as hydrogen, helium, water vapor, or simple molecules like carbon monoxide. Instead, it underscores how extreme environments can give rise to exotic cloud chemistry, including the formation of refractory condensates that would melt or vaporise under Earth‑like conditions. Similar mineral clouds have been hypothesized for other ultra‑hot super‑Earths and lava worlds, but direct spectroscopic evidence has been elusive until now. The presence of such “gemstone” clouds also has implications for the planet’s albedo—its reflectivity—and could influence how much heat is radiated back into space, thereby affecting atmospheric dynamics and potential weather patterns.

Beyond the immediate scientific intrigue, the finding opens new avenues for probing the composition of rocky exoplanets that are otherwise too distant for direct imaging. By cataloguing the specific minerals that condense in these extreme atmospheres, astronomers can infer the bulk composition of the underlying rock, offering a remote “spectroscopic geology” of worlds beyond our solar neighbourhood. This technique could eventually help distinguish between planets that are iron‑rich, silicate‑dominated, or possess exotic mineralogies, informing models of planet formation and migration.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to target a broader sample of ultra‑hot planets with next‑generation telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the upcoming Atmospheric Remote‑Sensing Infrared Exoplanet Large‑Survey (ARIEL) mission. With higher sensitivity and broader wavelength coverage, future observations may reveal a richer diversity of mineral clouds, perhaps even detecting signatures of more exotic compounds like titanium oxide or iron‑bearing silicates. As instrumentation improves, the once‑theoretical notion of “gemstone” atmospheres may become a routine aspect of exoplanet science, reshaping our perception of how planets behave under the most extreme conditions the universe can offer.
